subject: AP World History: Modern
source_note: Structured from the AP World History: Modern Course and Exam Description (© 2026). Unit titles and date ranges follow the CED's own framework. The essential questions are written for this app and are not the CED's; skill descriptions are paraphrased rather than quoted.

units.title: Unit 1: The Global Tapestry (c. 1200–1450)
essential_questions: Song China, Dar al-Islam, and the Delhi Sultanate all held power over people who did not share the ruler's faith. What did each rely on to make that work, and which looks most fragile to you?
Was the state in this period mainly an instrument of extraction, or of order? Pick one region and argue it.
If you had to name the single most important source of a ruler's legitimacy in 1300, what would it be — and where does your answer break down?
focus_skills: State precisely what changed, where, and when — name the development, do not gesture at it
Separate what a source asserts from what it actually shows, and weigh the evidence behind it
Place a development in the wider world of its moment — what else was under way, and where
Make a defensible claim, support it with specific evidence, and answer the strongest objection
texts: Whatever primary sources you are reading for this unit — bring the text and we will work from it

units.title: Unit 2: Networks of Exchange (c. 1200–1450)
essential_questions: The Silk Roads, the Indian Ocean, and the trans-Saharan routes all moved goods. Which moved ideas most effectively, and what about it did that?
Was the Mongol Empire better for trade than it was destructive to the places it conquered? Defend a position.
Merchants carried disease as readily as silk. Does that make these networks a net gain for the people living along them?
focus_skills: State precisely what changed, where, and when — name the development, do not gesture at it
Work out who made a source, for whom, and why, and say how that shapes what it claims
Place a development in the wider world of its moment — what else was under way, and where
Set two things side by side and account for the difference, the cause, or what persisted
Make a defensible claim, support it with specific evidence, and answer the strongest objection
texts: Travel accounts and merchant records for this unit — paste the passage you are working from

units.title: Unit 3: Land-Based Empires (c. 1450–1750)
essential_questions: Gunpowder gets the credit for these empires. What else was doing the work, and how would you show it mattered more?
The Ottomans, Safavids, and Mughals all ruled religiously mixed populations. Whose approach would you call most durable, and by what measure?
Is 'gunpowder empire' a useful category or a label that flattens real differences? Argue one way.

units.title: Unit 4: Transoceanic Interconnections (c. 1450–1750)
essential_questions: The Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals, people, and pathogens. Which of those changed the most lives, and how would you defend that against the others?
Was European maritime expansion driven more by technology, by state competition, or by demand for Asian goods? Rank them and justify the order.
Silver from Potosí ended up in China. What does that single fact let you argue about the world economy in 1600?

units.title: Unit 5: Revolutions (c. 1750–1900)
essential_questions: Enlightenment ideas were available to many societies. Why did they produce revolution in some places and not others?
Britain industrialised first. Was that geography, institutions, coal, or empire? Make the case for one and name what it cannot explain.
The Haitian Revolution used the same language as the French. Why is it remembered so differently?

units.title: Unit 6: Consequences of Industrialization (c. 1750–1900)
essential_questions: Imperialism was justified by civilising language and driven by economics. Which explanation does the evidence support better?
Industrialisation raised output and shortened lives in the same cities. How do you weigh those against each other?
Did resistance to empire ever change how empire operated, or only how it described itself?

units.title: Unit 7: Global Conflict (c. 1900–present)
essential_questions: Total war required states to reach into ordinary life as never before. Did that expansion of state power ever really recede?
Was the Second World War a continuation of the First, or a different conflict? Argue it with evidence, not assertion.
Colonial troops fought in both wars. What did that do to the empires that recruited them?

units.title: Unit 8: Cold War and Decolonization (c. 1900–present)
essential_questions: Newly independent states chose alignment, non-alignment, or something in between. What decided which?
Was the Cold War primarily an ideological contest or a great-power rivalry that used ideology? Pick one.
Decolonisation transferred sovereignty. How much did it transfer power?

units.title: Unit 9: Globalization (c. 1900–present)
essential_questions: Technology shrank distance. Has it made the world more alike, or made differences more visible?
Who has actually benefited from global economic integration? Answer with a specific case, not a generalisation.
Climate change is a global problem produced unequally. What does that do to arguments about who should act?
